Belgium. A nation in northwestern Europe at the crossroads of French, German, and Dutch-speaking cultures, making it a strategic flashpoint in European history. Belgium was created in eighteen thirty as an independent state following the Belgian Revolution against Dutch rule. Before independence, it had been part of the Spanish Netherlands, then the Austrian Netherlands, then annexed by France and Holland.

The nation remains divided between Flemish-speaking Flanders in the north and French-speaking Wallonia in the south. This linguistic division has driven political tension and decentralization throughout Belgian history. Belgium became an early industrial power in the nineteenth century. Coal mining, textile manufacturing, and steel production fueled rapid urbanization and working-class unrest.

King Leopold the Second, who reigned from eighteen sixty-five to nineteen nine, established the Belgian Congo as his personal colonial property in Central Africa. There, Belgian exploitation, forced labor, and resource extraction killed an estimated ten million Africans. This legacy would stain Belgian historical memory permanently.

Belgium was overrun and occupied by Germany during World War One from nineteen fourteen to nineteen eighteen. The Western Front's trench warfare devastated Belgian territory and killed over one hundred thousand Belgian soldiers. Germany invaded Belgium again during World War Two in nineteen forty, leading to four years of occupation. Belgium was liberated by Allied forces in nineteen forty-four.

After World War Two, Belgium became a founding member of NATO and the European Union. Brussels became the seat of European Union institutions, making Belgium central to European integration and peace.
